parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ellersby**
> 
> Ellersby manufactures office furniture in country G. It currently makes its own metal frames and is considering buying them from an outside supplier instead.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows Ellersby's statement of profit or loss for 2026 and the directors' forecast for 2027 if frames are bought in.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Ellersby statement of profit or loss (\$000)**
> 
> |   | 2026 actual | 2027 forecast |
> |---|---|---|
> | Revenue | 9 400 | 9 400 |
> | Cost of sales | 6 110 | 5 640 |
> | **Gross profit** | **3 290** | **3 760** |
> | Expenses | 2 820 | 3 015 |
> | **Profit from operations** | **470** | **745** |
> 
> The 2027 forecast includes redundancy payments of \$390 000 to the 14 employees who make frames. Without those payments, expenses would fall to \$2 625 000.
> 
> The supplier is the only business in country G able to make the frames to Ellersby's specification. It quotes a seven-week lead time; Ellersby currently offers its corporate customers four weeks, which is its main selling point.

Evaluate whether Ellersby should buy in its metal frames rather than making them.
parts.solution_md:
The statement of profit or loss shows the effect of the change on each line of trading **[K]**. Buying frames in would cut cost of sales from \$6 110 000 to \$5 640 000, raising gross profit from \$3 290 000 to \$3 760 000, while profit from operations would rise from \$470 000 to \$745 000 **[Ap]**. That is an increase of 59% in a single year, achieved even though the forecast carries \$390 000 of redundancy payments that will not recur **[An]**. Excluding those, expenses would be \$2 625 000 rather than \$3 015 000, so from 2028 profit from operations would be around \$1 135 000, more than double the current figure **[An]**

The forecast rests on an assumption the statement cannot test **[K]**. Revenue is held at \$9 400 000, yet the supplier quotes seven weeks against the four Ellersby currently offers, and that lead time is its main selling point with corporate customers **[Ap]**. If even a tenth of revenue were lost, \$940 000 of sales would disappear, and at the forecast gross margin of 40% that removes \$376 000 of gross profit, more than wiping out the year-one gain of \$275 000 **[An]**. Once frame-making has stopped and 14 employees have been paid off the decision cannot easily be reversed, so a fall in revenue would be discovered only after the capacity to correct it has gone **[An]**

On the figures alone Ellersby should buy in **[E]**. The saving is large, it recurs every year, and the redundancy cost is a one-off the forecast has already absorbed **[E]**. What makes the decision finely balanced is that the whole case depends on revenue holding at \$9 400 000, and the change most likely to break that assumption, a lead time rising from four weeks to seven, is precisely what Ellersby sells on **[E]**. There is also no second supplier in country G, so Ellersby would have no alternative if prices rose later and the savings shown here could be reclaimed by the supplier over time **[E]**. Ellersby should therefore not commit yet: it should establish with its largest corporate customers whether seven weeks is acceptable, and negotiate a fixed-price agreement of several years before closing frame production **[E]**. If lead times can be protected, perhaps by holding frame inventory, the change is clearly worth making; if they cannot, the profit gain is being bought with the business's main competitive advantage **[E]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Talgarth Scaffolding**
> 
> Talgarth Scaffolding hires out scaffolding to builders in country V. It has asked its bank for a loan of \$600 000 to buy new equipment.
> 
> Talgarth's directors have given the bank its statement of profit or loss, pointing out that profit for the year has risen from \$210 000 to \$340 000.
> 
> Three further facts are not obvious from the statement:
> 
> - \$180 000 of the 2026 profit came from selling a depot that Talgarth no longer needed
> - Talgarth changed its depreciation policy in 2026, extending the assumed useful life of its scaffolding from five years to eight, which reduced the annual depreciation charge by \$70 000
> - Two large customers now take 90 days to pay rather than 30
> 
> Anya, the bank's lending manager, must decide whether the statement of profit or loss gives her enough information.

Evaluate the usefulness of Talgarth Scaffolding's statement of profit or loss to the bank in deciding whether to lend.
parts.solution_md:
A statement of profit or loss shows revenue, costs and the profit earned over a period **[K]**. Talgarth's profit for the year rose from \$210 000 to \$340 000, and this is the figure the directors have put to the bank **[Ap]**. Taken at face value it describes a business whose earnings grew by 62% in a year, which would make this a straightforward lending decision **[An]**. The statement is useful to Anya precisely because it reduces a year of trading to a single comparable figure, and no other document does that job **[An]**

The difficulty is what that figure contains **[K]**. \$180 000 of the 2026 profit came from selling a depot, and a further \$70 000 from extending the assumed life of scaffolding from five years to eight **[Ap]**. Neither has anything to do with hiring scaffolding out: a depot can only be sold once, and the depreciation change is an accounting judgement rather than a change in performance **[An]**. Stripping both out leaves around \$90 000 of profit from trading, well below the \$210 000 earned in 2025, so the statement reports growth in a business that has actually declined **[An]**

The statement is therefore useful but not sufficient **[E]**. It gives Anya the right starting point, and read carefully it is what allows the one-off gain and the policy change to be identified at all, so the fault lies with the directors' presentation rather than the document **[E]**. What it cannot tell her is whether Talgarth will generate the cash to make repayments, and with two large customers now taking 90 days rather than 30, profit and cash are moving apart **[E]**. A lender is repaid out of cash, not profit, so a statement of profit or loss can never be the whole basis of the decision **[E]**. Anya should use it as evidence of trading performance across several years, adjusted for the one-off items, and require a cash flow forecast and the statement of financial position before committing \$600 000 **[E]**

> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one use of the statement of profit or loss in context |

> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |

> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The statement is useful because it summarises a whole year's trading in one figure that can be compared with previous years, showing revenue, costs and profit separately so the bank can see where earnings come from. However, \$180 000 of the 2026 profit came from a one-off depot sale that cannot be repeated, so the headline figure does not describe trading at all
> - Comparison across years reveals trends a single year cannot, and the statement is prepared to a consistent format allowing comparison with other businesses. However, extending asset lives from five to eight years cut depreciation by \$70 000 and flattered profit without any change in performance, so this year is not comparable with last on a consistent basis
> - Adjusted for both items, trading profit is around \$90 000 against \$210 000 the previous year, which reverses the picture the directors have presented. However, the statement itself is what makes those adjustments possible, so the document is sound even though the presentation is not
> - Profit is not cash, and two customers moving from 30 to 90 days weakens the cash position from which a loan is actually repaid. However, longer terms may have been granted to win or retain large customers, so the change is not necessarily a sign of weakness
> - The statement says nothing about assets available as security, which the statement of financial position would show, and it is historic while the bank is lending against future performance. However, no single document answers every question, and past trading is the best available evidence about future trading
> - Anya could require a cash flow forecast and the statement of financial position before deciding. However, forecasts are prepared by the same directors whose presentation has already proved selective, so additional documents do not remove the need for scepticism
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Wexford Signs**
> 
> Wexford Signs designs and installs illuminated shop signs in country H.
> 
> Wexford has agreed to buy the workshop it currently rents. The purchase removes annual rent of \$84 000, but Wexford will take a loan of \$700 000 at 7% interest a year, and the building will be depreciated at \$28 000 a year using the straight-line method.
> 
> The directors expect no change to revenue or cost of sales.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows Wexford's most recent statement of profit or loss.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Wexford Signs statement of profit or loss, year ended 2026 (\$)**
> 
> | Revenue | 1 640 000 |
> |---|---|
> | Cost of sales | 902 000 |
> | **Gross profit** | **738 000** |
> | Expenses | 601 000 |
> | **Profit from operations** | **137 000** |
> | Interest | 19 000 |
> | **Profit for the year** | **118 000** |

Analyse the impact of buying the workshop on Wexford Signs' statement of profit or loss.
parts.solution_md:
Buying the workshop changes two items within expenses **[K]**. Wexford's rent of \$84 000 disappears, but straight-line depreciation of \$28 000 on the building appears in its place, so expenses fall by \$56 000 from \$601 000 to \$545 000 **[Ap]**. With revenue and cost of sales unchanged, gross profit stays at \$738 000 and profit from operations rises by that same \$56 000, from \$137 000 to \$193 000 **[An]**. On the operating line alone the purchase looks clearly worthwhile, because Wexford replaces a payment that would continue indefinitely with a charge that is smaller and spread across the building's life **[An]** Most of that gain disappears below the operating line **[K]**. The \$700 000 loan carries interest at 7%, adding \$49 000 a year to the existing \$19 000 **[Ap]**. Profit for the year therefore rises only from \$118 000 to \$125 000, an improvement of \$7 000, because interest absorbs \$49 000 of the \$56 000 saved **[An]**. The statement makes clear that this is a financing decision as much as a property decision, since almost the whole benefit visible at operating level is transferred to the lender before it reaches the bottom line **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ormesby**
> 
> Ormesby manufactures workwear for construction and healthcare businesses in country K.
> 
> Two years ago Ormesby moved to a cheaper fabric supplier and raised its prices by 6%. It also opened a showroom and increased its sales team from 4 people to 11.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows extracts from Ormesby's statement of profit or loss.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Ormesby statement of profit or loss extracts (\$000)**
> 
> |   | 2024 | 2026 |
> |---|---|---|
> | Revenue | 4 200 | 4 750 |
> | Cost of sales | 2 940 | 3 087 |
> | **Gross profit** | **1 260** | **1 663** |
> | Expenses | 890 | 1 430 |
> | **Profit from operations** | **370** | **233** |

Analyse **two** aspects of Ormesby's performance shown by its statement of profit or loss.
parts.solution_md:
The statement of profit or loss separates gross profit, which is revenue less cost of sales, from profit from operations, which deducts expenses as well **[K]**. Ormesby's gross profit rose from \$1 260 000 to \$1 663 000 and its gross profit margin from 30% to 35% **[Ap]**. This shows the two decisions affecting cost of sales have worked: the cheaper fabric reduced the cost of each garment while the 6% price rise increased revenue per garment, and together they widened the gap between what Ormesby charges and what production costs **[An]**. Judged on trading alone Ormesby performed better in 2026 than in 2024, and the improvement is in margin rather than simply in volume **[An]** The picture reverses below gross profit **[K]**. Expenses rose from \$890 000 to \$1 430 000, an increase of 61%, and profit from operations fell from \$370 000 to \$233 000 **[Ap]**. The showroom and the growth of the sales team from 4 to 11 are indirect costs appearing as expenses rather than cost of sales, so they leave the gross margin untouched while consuming more than the entire gross profit gain **[An]**. Ormesby has spent \$540 000 more on selling in order to win \$550 000 more revenue, so the expansion is generating almost no additional profit and the business is working considerably harder for less **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** reason why a business charges depreciation in its accounts.
parts.solution_md:
Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset across the years in which the business uses it **[1]**. Without it, the full cost of a machine expected to last eight years would be charged to the year it was bought, making that year's profit look artificially low and the following seven look artificially high **[1]**. Charging depreciation each year matches the cost to the revenue the asset helps to earn, so profit gives a fairer picture of performance in every year rather than being distorted by when the purchase happened **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life
> 
> AO2
> 
> - It matches the cost of the asset to the periods in which it generates revenue
> - Without it, profit is badly distorted in the year of purchase and overstated afterwards
> - It reduces the carrying value of the asset so the statement of financial position is not overstated
> - It recognises that assets lose value through use, age and obsolescence
> - It allows fairer comparison of profit between years and between businesses
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Depreciation is not cash. No money leaves the business when it is charged, and nothing is being saved up to replace the asset; the cash went when the asset was bought. Answers claiming a business "sets money aside through depreciation" lose marks, so keep your explanation about spreading a cost that has already been paid.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** way in which a supplier could use a business's statement of financial position.
parts.solution_md:
A statement of financial position shows what a business owns and owes at a particular date **[1]**. A supplier deciding whether to offer trade credit would compare current assets with current liabilities, because that indicates whether the business can meet its short-term debts **[1]**. If current liabilities are close to or above current assets, the supplier risks not being paid and may insist on payment in advance or refuse credit altogether, which directly affects the terms the business is offered **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and equity at a specific date
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Comparing current assets with current liabilities indicates whether short-term debts can be met
> - A supplier can judge whether to offer trade credit, and on what terms
> - High non-current liabilities may show the business is already heavily committed to lenders
> - Comparing two years shows whether the position is improving or deteriorating
> - A weak position may lead a supplier to require payment in advance, cut credit limits or decline the order
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Match the user to the figure they would actually look at. A supplier's concern is whether it will be paid, so it goes straight to current assets and current liabilities, not to the equity section. Answers that describe the whole statement rather than the part that stakeholder cares about tend to stall at one mark.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** difficulty a business may face when valuing its inventory.
parts.solution_md:
Inventory is normally valued at the lower of what it cost and what the business expects to receive for it **[1]**. A difficulty arises with items whose value falls sharply over time, such as fashion clothing at the end of a season **[1]**. The business must estimate what that stock will eventually sell for, and if it judges this too optimistically the inventory is overstated on the statement of financial position and profit is reported as higher than it really is **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, which requires an estimate
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Items that go out of fashion or perish may be worth far less than they cost, and the fall is a matter of judgement
> - Work in progress is difficult to value because it is unfinished and has no established selling price
> - Where identical items were bought at different prices, the business must choose which cost to apply
> - Damaged or obsolete stock may still be recorded at full cost if nobody identifies it
> - Estimating selling costs, such as the discounts needed to shift slow-moving lines, is uncertain
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the kind of stock. "Inventory can be hard to value" simply restates the question, whereas fashion clothing, fresh food or half-finished products each carry their own reason why the right figure is unclear. Choosing a specific type gives you something concrete to explain and makes the third mark far easier to reach.

Net realisable value is the amount a business expects to receive from selling an item of inventory **[1]**, after deducting any costs still needed to complete it and sell it **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The expected selling price of inventory less the costs of completing and selling it
> - The amount a business would actually realise from disposing of inventory, net of the costs of doing so
> - An estimate of what inventory is genuinely worth if sold, rather than what it originally cost
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not define the term by the rule it appears in. "The lower of cost and net realisable value" describes how inventory is valued; it does not say what net realisable value means, and on its own it earns nothing. Give the meaning first: the expected proceeds, minus the costs of getting them.

parts.problem_md: Explain how the statement of profit or loss is linked to the statement of financial position.
parts.solution_md:
The statement of profit or loss shows the profit earned over a period, while the statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and equity at the end of that period **[1]**. The two are joined by retained earnings, because profit not paid out as dividends is added to the reserves shown within equity **[1]**. A profitable year therefore increases equity on the statement of financial position without any new investment by shareholders, which is why the two statements have to be read together rather than separately **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Retained earnings link the two statements, carrying profit from one into equity in the other
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Profit not distributed as dividends increases reserves within equity
> - A loss reduces retained earnings and therefore reduces equity
> - Depreciation charged in the statement of profit or loss reduces the carrying value of non-current assets
> - Inventory valued at the year end appears as a current asset and also determines cost of sales
> - Together they show both performance over the year and position at the end of it
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A question about how two documents are linked wants the item that appears in both. Describing what each statement contains, however accurately, does not answer it. Name the connecting figure, usually retained earnings, then say which direction it travels.

A non-current asset is an item owned by a business that it expects to keep and use for more than one year **[1]**, such as machinery, vehicles or premises, rather than something bought in order to be sold on **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An asset the business intends to use for longer than one year rather than sell within it
> - A long-term resource such as property, machinery, equipment or vehicles
> - An item held for use in the business rather than as inventory for resale
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The time test does most of the work, but add the purpose test too. A delivery van is a non-current asset to a bakery and inventory to the dealership selling it; the same object is classified differently depending on why it is held. "Kept for more than a year and used in the business, not sold" covers both.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'statement of financial position'.
parts.solution_md:
A statement of financial position is a financial document showing what a business owns and owes at a particular date **[1]**, setting out its assets, liabilities and equity so its overall financial position at that moment can be seen **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A statement listing a business's assets, liabilities and equity at one specific date
> - A summary of what a business owns and what it owes at a given point in time
> - A financial statement showing how a business's assets have been funded, by liabilities or by equity
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the moment. A statement of financial position describes a single date, while a statement of profit or loss covers a whole period, and that difference is often the second mark. Writing "over the year" instead of "at the year end" quietly turns a correct definition into the wrong statement.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** reason why a public limited company must publish its financial statements.
parts.solution_md:
A public limited company has limited liability, which means its shareholders are not personally responsible for its debts **[1]**. Because those dealing with the company cannot pursue the owners' private assets if it fails, the law requires it to publish financial statements so anyone considering trading with it or investing in it can judge its financial position **[1]**. Publication is in effect the price of limited liability, giving suppliers, lenders and shareholders the information they need to decide whether to take that risk **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Public limited companies are legally required to publish their financial statements each year
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Limited liability protects shareholders' personal assets, so creditors need published information to assess the risk of dealing with the company
> - Shareholders who do not run the business need an account of how their money has been used
> - Potential investors require reliable information before buying shares
> - Lenders use the statements to judge whether the company can repay borrowing
> - Publication allows tax authorities to check the profit declared
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A question asking why a company must do something is about the obligation, not the advantage. An answer explaining that publishing is useful can still miss marks if it never reaches the point that this is a legal requirement flowing from limited liability. Deal with the "must" first, then explain who benefits.

parts.problem_md:
‘The published accounts of a public limited company are only useful to internal stakeholders.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solution_md:
Published accounts are useful to internal stakeholders in some ways. Shareholders can check the company's profit and dividend **[K]** to see the return on their investment, and employees might look at the accounts to judge whether a pay rise is likely **[An]**. Managers can also use trends in the published accounts, such as changing revenue or profit over time, to help with future financial planning **[An]** External stakeholders also rely on them heavily, often more than internal stakeholders do. A bank **[K] **deciding whether to lend money to a public limited company would use the published accounts to judge whether the company can afford to repay a loan **[Ap]** **[An]**. Potential investors use them to decide whether buying shares is a good investment, and the government uses them to work out how much tax the company owes. These external groups usually have no other way of finding out this information, so published accounts may actually matter more to them than to internal stakeholders **[E]** It is also worth noting that managers, as internal stakeholders, often have access to much more detailed financial information **[K]** than what is published, such as the profitability of individual departments. This means the published accounts themselves may be of limited extra use to managers specifically, even though they are internal stakeholders **[An]**. This weakens the idea that published accounts are especially useful to internal stakeholders as a group **[E]** Overall, I disagree with the statement **[E]**. Published accounts are clearly useful to a wide range of external stakeholders, such as banks, investors and government, who depend on them as one of their only sources of financial information about the company **[An]**. PC is a public limited company. Its head office is in Europe and it operates with centralised decision making. The company owns the Pop Cool brand name, logo and the distinctive bottle shape that is still used in some markets. PC operates its own bottling and canning factories in some countries. Consumer spending has fallen due to declining real incomes. There are ageing populations in most of the countries where PC sells its products. A loss of competitiveness in many industrial sectors has resulted in rising unemployment. Statement of financial position valuations Since 2008 PC’s share price has fallen. This has been the trend for many public limited companies. PC’s Finance Director has been considering three changes that will affect PC’s accounts. He could make all three changes or just one or two of them. • When calculating depreciation of new production equipment bought last year for \$25m, use an estimated life of 8 years not 5 years. We would then have all of the production facilities and distribution channels through large supermarkets that we will need. The existing brand names could then be replaced with the Pop Cool brand which we would advertise very heavily for a short period. Consumers will be attracted to this because it is so popular elsewhere in the world.’ Suzy replied: ‘There could be local opposition to this globalised approach – although the marketing economies of scale will be substantial. I think we should develop a range of soft drinks to suit local tastes with brand names that reflect local language and culture. We could distribute these new drinks through small retail stores and street markets. This way we will slowly but steadily build up consumer awareness and loyalty.’

Workforce planning in country X Country X is one of PC’s biggest markets. The company fully owns all of the production facilities in this country and it has a large sales and marketing team too. Another option is to introduce even more automation at our main packaging plant.’ The other managers agreed with him that meeting this new company objective of reducing labour costs was going to need careful workforce planning. Future options for PC’s growth PC’s Board of Directors has been criticised by the newspapers and by major shareholders for the company’s slow rate of growth in sales and profits since 2008. Option A: Develop new flavours and distinctive names for a wider range of PC products. The Marketing Director believes that much clearer market segmentation is the best strategy for achieving market penetration and higher profits.
